title: Gandhi and the Textile Labour Association
author: Editorial Desk
summary: For Gandhi Jayanti: the 1918 Ahmedabad strike, the Textile Labour Association, and the questions its method of arbitration and welfare still raises.
body:
On 2 October the nation remembers **Mahatma Gandhi**. In the history of Indian labour, he is remembered above all for his work in Ahmedabad, where a dispute between mill owners and textile workers in 1918 led to the formation of the **Textile Labour Association (TLA)**, formally inaugurated in 1920. The TLA became one of the longest-lived unions in the country and a model of a particular style of unionism: arbitration before strikes, self-reliance, and welfare work alongside bargaining. This post tells that story and asks what it still has to say to unions today.

## Background: Ahmedabad in 1917 and 1918

Ahmedabad was a major centre of textile mills. In 1917 a plague epidemic struck the city and, according to one account, killed close to a tenth of its population. To stop workers from fleeing, mill owners paid a "plague bonus", in some cases as high as 80 per cent of wages. When the owners planned to withdraw the bonus in January 1918, workers asked for a dearness allowance instead, since wartime inflation had roughly doubled the prices of food grains, cloth and other necessities ([Swarthmore Global Nonviolent Action Database](https://nvdatabase.swarthmore.edu/content/ahmedabad-textile-laborers-win-strike-economic-justice-1918)).

The workers turned to Anasuya Sarabhai, a social worker whose brother, Ambalal Sarabhai, headed the Mill Owners' Association. She approached Mohandas Gandhi, who was respected by both sides, and he proposed an arbitration board with three representatives from each side. The first attempt at arbitration failed because of mutual distrust. On 22 February 1918 the owners locked out the mills and offered work only to those who accepted a 20 per cent wage increase. After studying the industry, wages in Bombay and workers' living conditions, Gandhi judged a 35 per cent increase to be a fair demand ([Swarthmore database](https://nvdatabase.swarthmore.edu/content/ahmedabad-textile-laborers-win-strike-economic-justice-1918)).

## What happened: the strike, the fast and the settlement

Workers took a pledge to remain peaceful and not to return to work until their demand was met. There were daily public meetings, and welfare activities such as sanitation lessons and medical aid. As some workers began to drift back to the mills and morale weakened, Gandhi began a fast on 15 March 1918. By the third day he had proposed that the dispute be settled by an impartial arbitrator, Professor Anandshanker Dhruva, with compromise on details in the interim. The owners accepted on 18 March and the workers returned under an interim arrangement while the arbitrator decided. The arbitrator ultimately awarded the 35 per cent increase ([Swarthmore database](https://nvdatabase.swarthmore.edu/content/ahmedabad-textile-laborers-win-strike-economic-justice-1918)).

A history of the TLA published by the V.V. Giri National Labour Institute describes Gandhi's role as leading a strike of about three weeks in 1918 that established the principle of arbitration. It dates the roots of the union to a warpers' strike of 4 December 1917, which the workers still mark each year as Majoor Din, or Labour Day, and says the association was formally inaugurated by Gandhi on 25 February 1920 under a neem tree in the compound of Anasuyabehn Sarabhai at Mirzapur ([VVGNLI, Six Decades of Textile Labour Association](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Six%20Decades%20of%20Textile%20Labour%20Association%2C%20Ahmedabad%20%281917-1977%29.pdf)). Sources differ on the exact year of "founding", depending on whether one counts the first organising or the formal inauguration, which is why it is safest to say that the TLA grew out of the events of 1917 and 1918 and was formally inaugurated in 1920.

## The method

The VVGNLI history lists the guidelines that Gandhi gave to the union, which can be summarised as follows:

- **Reasonable demands, and willingness to compromise.** Ask for what can be justified, and be ready to settle.
- **Strike only as a last resort.** Use negotiation, conciliation and arbitration first, and strike only after they fail.
- **Non-violence**, even under provocation.
- **Self-reliance.** Do not depend on outside donations.
- **Oppose the employers' policy, not the employer as a person.**
- **Build character** through education and constructive work.

This is often connected with Gandhi's wider idea of "trusteeship", the view that owners hold wealth in trust for society. The VVGNLI history I consulted does not discuss trusteeship, so that link should be treated as a commentary on Gandhi's thought, not as a documented rule of the union ([VVGNLI](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Six%20Decades%20of%20Textile%20Labour%20Association%2C%20Ahmedabad%20%281917-1977%29.pdf)).

## Structure, size and welfare work

The TLA began as a federation of 12 occupational unions, and Anasuyabehn Sarabhai served as its first and lifelong president. Shankarlal Banker was a long-serving adviser. By the institute's figures the union had about 1,04,000 members in 1947 and about 1,25,423 in April 1976, in an industry with 65 mills and roughly 1,33,275 workers at the time of the study ([VVGNLI](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Six%20Decades%20of%20Textile%20Labour%20Association%2C%20Ahmedabad%20%281917-1977%29.pdf)). A union that enrols the great majority of workers in an industry in a city is in a strong position to bargain, and the TLA's record shows it.

What distinguished the TLA was the range of its welfare work, funded largely by workers themselves. The history records a school for workers' children started in 1914, night schools, nursery classes, libraries and reading centres, a labour hospital, a maternity home named after Kasturba Gandhi, dispensaries, and co-operative housing societies under which workers built about 20,000 houses. In 1947 the union founded the Majoor Sahakari Bank, which by 1977 had more than 48,000 members ([VVGNLI](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Six%20Decades%20of%20Textile%20Labour%20Association%2C%20Ahmedabad%20%281917-1977%29.pdf)). In other words, the union looked after education, health, housing and savings as well as wages. Anasuya Sarabhai herself began social work among mill workers' families before the 1918 strike, and later founded a school for mill girls in 1927 ([Wikipedia: Anasuya Sarabhai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anasuya_Sarabhai)).

## Why it matters to BMS and to us

The TLA is an early example of a union that wanted to be independent of party politics and that worked for both a fair wage and the welfare of the worker's family. BMS's own literature stresses similar themes. Its pamphlet describes BMS as a genuine trade union rooted in nationalism and meant to stay clear of party politics, built from the grassroots with no inherited members or funds, and it describes a "responsive cooperation" approach to any elected Government ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). BMS also rejects class struggle as a theory and speaks of the "industrial family". The TLA and BMS are different organisations with different histories, and we do not suggest that one is a copy of the other, but readers who study both will notice shared concerns: independence, constructive work and settlement through dialogue.

## Questions Gandhi's model raises

- **Can arbitration replace strikes in all cases?** Today's Industrial Relations Code gives workers the right to strike but requires notice, and it sets up a system of conciliation and tribunals. The Labour Ministry's summary of the Codes describes two-member industrial tribunals with direct access after conciliation ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf)). Gandhi's idea that strike should follow, not replace, dialogue is built into the structure of the law, though unions differ on how well it works in practice.
- **How can a union stay independent of party politics yet influence policy?** The TLA answered by building its own strength and its own welfare institutions. The modern equivalent is serious research, well-prepared memoranda and presence in tripartite bodies.
- **How do we balance workers' rights and the industry's health?** The 1918 settlement gave workers a substantial increase, and the arbitrator cited the mills' large profits during the war. The point is that a fair claim rests on facts about the industry's capacity to pay.
- **Where should a union's welfare work stop?** Schools, hospitals and banks require management and money. They are worth doing, but only if they are run with honesty and transparency.

## For further study

Anyone interested should read the VVGNLI history of the TLA, which is freely available, and the biography of Anasuya Sarabhai. Both show how a union can be built slowly, member by member, and how its character depends on its leaders and rules as much as its numbers. These questions remain live, and every union answers them in its own way.
